Twenty Years of Seeing the Universe: How Space Imaging Grew Up

From a CubeSat's snapshot of Earth to a map of the invisible forces around it — tracing two decades of detector work behind some of ESA and NASA's biggest missions, through the Open University's Centre for Electronic Imaging.

MOCKUP — for internal review

Twenty years ago, a spacecraft camera was still, fundamentally, a camera: point it, expose it, get a picture back. Today, the instruments flying on the biggest ESA and NASA missions barely resemble that idea. Some build a three-dimensional map from a billion individual measurements rather than a single frame; others catch X-rays too faint for any conventional sensor, or infrared light revealing worlds no eye could ever see directly. Tracing that shift means tracing the detectors underneath it. Few places have had a hand in as many as the Open University's Centre for Electronic Imaging (CEI), whose sensors, developed with Teledyne e2v, have flown on more than 200 missions over the past two decades.

CEI's role is rarely to build a spacecraft; it is to understand how detectors will behave once exposed to the radiation of deep space, and to make sure they still perform after years of that battering. That work has run alongside almost every major shift in what space imaging can do. It began simply, with a picture of Earth. UKube-1, the UK Space Agency's first CubeSat, launched in 2014 carrying CEI's Compact CMOS Camera Demonstrator, C3D — three imagers packed into a shoebox-sized satellite, including a wide-field camera picturing the whole of Earth at around 350 m resolution and a narrow-field imager reaching roughly 25 m. It was the first flight of this generation of European CMOS sensor technology, proof that a sensor could survive orbit and still take a recognisable photograph.

From there, the idea of what a space "image" even is began to stretch. Gaia, in orbit since 2013, uses its CCDs to time the transit of starlight to extraordinary precision rather than photograph stars directly, and CEI's contribution has been modelling how radiation damage distorts those measurements over the mission's life. The payoff is a three-dimensional map of nearly two billion stars across the Milky Way, assembled entirely from data rather than a camera shutter — precise enough to catch the disc still rippling from a past close encounter with a smaller galaxy, oscillations astronomers now study as galactic seismology to reconstruct events in the Milky Way's history that no photograph could show. Space imaging had stopped being only about pictures and started reconstructing what the eye could never see.

Euclid, ESA's dark-universe mission launched in 2023, pushed the same idea further, building an instrument to survey billions of galaxies precisely enough to map the invisible scaffolding of dark matter holding them together and trace the dark energy driving the universe's runaway expansion, not to photograph any single one. CEI spent fifteen years characterising and calibrating the 36 CCD273-84 detectors in Euclid's visible-light instrument. CEI's Dr Jesper Skottfelt described the work as spanning nearly the mission's whole development. That effort is now visible in the sky: Euclid's Early Release Observations of 2024 and its first Quick Data Release in March 2025, both issued ahead of the mission's full Data Release 1, have already produced sweeping deep-field mosaics and sharp images of nearby galaxies, a preview of the billions of galaxies Euclid will eventually chart.

And sometimes the image is proof the camera still works, a billion kilometres from home. JUICE, the Jupiter Icy Moons Explorer launched in 2023, carries a CEI-built CMOS sensor, the CIS115, inside its JANUS camera. In August 2024, during a lunar-Earth flyby testing the spacecraft's instruments ahead of its long cruise to Jupiter, JANUS returned its first images: functional test frames of the Moon and Earth, some deliberately saturated or degraded to check how well its calibration algorithms could recover detail. They were engineering images rather than science images, but they confirmed that hardware tested at the Open University was working exactly as designed, on the way to the outer solar system.

That same arc — from Earth photographs, to star surveys, to dark-universe mosaics, to deep-space engineering tests — runs through missions beyond these four. CEI detectors have flown on India's Chandrayaan-1 and Chandrayaan-2 lunar missions, supporting X-ray spectrometry of the Moon's surface, and the centre works on ESA's PLATO exoplanet hunter, whose CCDs are among the largest ever built for space, plus the X- and gamma-ray missions THESEUS and OGRE and the ultraviolet spectrograph WSO-UVS — each still years from launch but already drawing on that same radiation-testing expertise.

That arc points next toward imaging forces, not just objects. SMILE, a joint ESA-Chinese Academy of Sciences mission, launched on a Vega-C rocket on 19 May 2026 and reached its highly elliptical science orbit in June. It carries a CEI-developed CCD at the heart of its Soft X-ray Imager, built to photograph Earth's magnetosphere directly for the first time as the solar wind collides with our planet's magnetic shield; with commissioning complete this August, its science campaign begins this very month, delivering the first global images of that invisible boundary.

The electron-multiplying CCDs whose radiation performance CEI has spent years characterising are also now in space, aboard NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, launched 30 August 2026 and travelling to a vantage point a million miles from Earth, with first images expected in early 2027 from a 300-megapixel infrared camera built to survey the sky roughly a thousand times faster than Hubble.

Further still, CEI is contributing detector research toward NASA's proposed Habitable Worlds Observatory, built to directly image Earth-like planets circling other stars, and continuing work on ESA's NewAthena, the rescoped X-ray observatory now proposed for launch in 2037, where CEI is developing radiation-shielding to cut background noise in its Wide Field Imager.

Lay the two decades end to end and the shift is stark. What began as a single photograph of Earth from a shoebox satellite has become surveys precise enough to hear the Milky Way ring like a bell and trace the dark matter and dark energy shaping the universe's structure. It is now becoming instruments sharp enough to resolve a planet circling another star, or, this year, to photograph the invisible magnetic shield wrapped around Earth itself for the first time. The next target for that same detector work is the faint, reflected light of another Earth.
